title: Cognitive Convergence: Deep Similarities Between Large Language Models and Human Cognition
summary: LLMs are widely regarded as alien intelligences, systems whose cognitive operations are fundamentally unlike our own. Apparent similarities to human cognition are therefore often seen as the result of anthropomorphic projection. We argue that this framing is mistaken. LLMs clearly differ from humans in important respects, including their physical substrate, learning history, and the environments with which they interact. These differences make it all the more striking that contemporary LLM-based systems converge with human cognition on a number of principles of cognitive organization with longstanding support in cognitive science. We identify structural correspondences across five dimensions: inferential organization, computational architecture, representational structure, prediction-driven learning, and reinforcement-learning-like mechanisms supporting goal-directed action. These correspondences support a broader model of intelligent cognition in which core principles long used to explain human intelligence also characterize contemporary LLM-based systems.

AI.tldr: Despite fundamental differences in substrate and learning history, LLMs and humans share key cognitive organizing principles across five dimensions (inference, architecture, representation, prediction-driven learning, and reinforcement-like mechanisms), challenging the view of LLMs as purely alien intelligences.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to challenge the dominant framing of LLMs as "alien intelligences" whose cognitive operations are fundamentally unlike human cognition, arguing instead that meaningful structural correspondences exist between LLM-based systems and human cognition.
AI.method: The paper identifies and compares structural correspondences across five dimensions of cognitive organization: inferential organization, computational architecture, representational structure, prediction-driven learning, and reinforcement-learning-like mechanisms supporting goal-directed action.
AI.result: Contemporary LLM-based systems converge with human cognition on multiple principles of cognitive organization that have longstanding support in cognitive science, despite clear differences in physical substrate, learning history, and environmental interaction.
AI.conclusion: Core principles long used to explain human intelligence also characterize contemporary LLM-based systems, supporting a broader model of intelligent cognition that bridges human and artificial cognition.

title: Three Failures of Pain Location: Why the Diagnostic Utility of Symptom Localization Is Not One Thing
summary: Patient-reported pain location is diagnostically decisive for some presentations and nearly uninformative for others. The prevailing account treats this as a single gradient of diagnostic utility governed by anatomical complexity. That explanation conflates three epistemically distinct failures of localization, each with its own mathematical structure, optimal instrument, and public-health consequence. In anatomical multiplexing (a), many structures share one location: a non-identifiable inverse problem. In delocalized amplification (b) --- clinically, central sensitization or nociplastic pain --- a centrally driven pain-behaviour pattern replaces the peripheral generator: a change of generative model. In referred/atypical displacement (c), location shifts in a systematic, person-dependent way, as in referred pain and in atypical presentations: a covariate-dependent bias. The three behave differently under inverse-problem, information-theoretic, decision-theoretic, and neural-field models, and demand different remedies. A single principle unifies them: they are one Bayesian inference problem failing at different nodes, meaning different points in one generative model: the likelihood, the model class, and the prior and loss. Observation over time increases the recoverable information. A fourth node, the report itself, carries this paper's main formal contribution --- a spatial Bayesian model of where pain is said to be, distinct from where it is felt. Re-examination further finds that the published "high-utility" accuracy band leans on overstated specificity, so the gradient is real but flatter than drawn. The account sits on a "why-location-fails" axis, a synthesis distinct from the nociceptive/neuropathic/nociplastic taxonomy (Kosek et al., 2016).

AI.tldr: This paper identifies three distinct ways pain location can be diagnostically misleading—anatomical multiplexing, delocalized amplification, and referred/atypical displacement—unified under a Bayesian inference framework, and argues the traditional "high-accuracy" diagnostic band is overstated.
AI.motivation: The prevailing view treats diagnostic utility of pain location as a single gradient based on anatomical complexity, conflating three epistemically distinct failure modes. The authors aim to disentangle these and provide a formal mathematical account.
AI.method: The paper employs inverse-problem, information-theoretic, decision-theoretic, and neural-field models; introduces a spatial Bayesian model distinguishing reported pain location from felt pain location; and re-examines published diagnostic accuracy data.
AI.result: Three distinct failure types (multiplexing, amplification, displacement) each have unique mathematical structure and require different remedies. The "high-utility" accuracy band is overstated due to inflated specificity. Observation over time improves recoverable information.
AI.conclusion: Pain location's diagnostic value is best understood via a "why-location-fails" axis within a Bayesian generative model (likelihood, model class, prior/loss nodes), offering a synthesis distinct from existing nociceptive/neuropathic/nociplastic taxonomies.

title: Artificial intelligence in deep brain stimulation for movement disorders: a systematic review and technology readiness assessment
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored across deep brain stimulation (DBS) for movement disorders, yet whether current systems are approaching deployment remains unclear. To characterise their scope, validation maturity, and translational readiness, we systematically evaluated 239 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2025, assessing AI methods, validation practices, and barriers constraining clinical translation. Research was dominated by Parkinson's disease and subthalamic nucleus targeting, with limited coverage of other disorders and targets. Most studies reported encouraging internal performance; however, external validation was rare, evaluations remained predominantly retrospective and single-centre, and more than one-quarter involved small-sample, high-dimensional datasets with elevated overfitting risk. Technology readiness assessment revealed that most systems remain at early-to-intermediate translational stages, constrained more by limited validation than by algorithmic inadequacy, compounded by the biological heterogeneity and dynamic complexity inherent to DBS. Nevertheless, emerging external and prospective studies suggest a field moving toward clinical maturity, with promising applications in targeting, programming, outcome prediction, and adaptive therapy delivery.

AI.tldr: This systematic review of 239 DBS-AI studies (2000-2025) finds that while AI methods show promising internal performance for movement disorders, most systems remain at early-to-intermediate translational stages due to limited external validation, small-sample high-dimensional datasets, and biological complexity—though emerging prospective studies signal movement toward clinical maturity.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the scope, validation maturity, and translational readiness of AI applications in DBS for movement disorders, given the gap between growing research interest and actual clinical deployment.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of 239 peer-reviewed studies (2000-2025) assessing AI methods, validation practices, and barriers to clinical translation, including technology readiness assessment.
AI.result: Research dominated by Parkinson's disease and subthalamic nucleus; internal performance encouraging but external validation rare; evaluations retrospective and single-centre; >1/4 studies had small-sample high-dimensional data with overfitting risk; most systems at early-to-intermediate translational stages; main constraint is limited validation rather than algorithmic inadequacy.
AI.conclusion: The field is constrained more by validation gaps than algorithmic issues, compounded by biological heterogeneity and dynamic complexity of DBS, but emerging external and prospective studies indicate movement toward clinical maturity with promising applications in targeting, programming, outcome prediction, and adaptive therapy.

title: Hybrid SINDy-EnKF in Learning Chikungunya Dynamics from Incomplete, Noisy or Partially Observed Data
summary: Current mechanistic models for the transmission dynamics of the Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) rely on uncertain parameters or partially observed data. This limitation challenges the use of theoretical models for understanding and forecasting disease spread. Here we present a hybrid, data-driven model framework that combines Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) with the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) for sequential data assimilation. Our numerical experiments show that this approach improves prediction accuracy and provides a good reconstruction of unobserved trajectories under partial observability, a common constraint in real-world epidemiological surveillance. SINDy can be applied to epidemic trajectories, recovering the underlying equations in noise-free conditions. However, standalone SINDy is highly sensitive to noise, leading to spurious terms and poor performance. Hence, we embed the identification procedure within an EnKF framework, which assimilates noisy observations to correct forecast states from the SINDy-derived model and to infer unobserved state variables.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid data-driven model combining SINDy and Ensemble Kalman Filter to improve Chikungunya virus transmission forecasting and reconstruct unobserved trajectories under noisy, partially observable conditions.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic models for CHIKV rely on uncertain parameters or partial data, limiting their use for forecasting. There is a need for a more robust approach that handles noise and partial observability in epidemiological surveillance.
AI.method: The authors combine SINDy (for equation discovery) with Ensemble Kalman Filter (for noise filtering and state assimilation). SINDy recovers underlying dynamics; EnKF corrects forecasts from noisy observations and infers unobserved variables.
AI.result: The hybrid SINDy-EnKF approach improves prediction accuracy and reconstructs unobserved trajectories under partial observability, outperforming standalone SINDy which is highly noise-sensitive.
AI.conclusion: Embedding SINDy within an EnKF framework provides a robust data-driven modeling tool for epidemic forecasting under realistic noisy and partially observed conditions.

title: A behavior-environment information loop drives sensory navigation
summary: As organisms navigate the environment to locate critical resources, their behavioral actions must be tightly coupled to their sensory inputs. Here, we introduce an information-theoretic framework that quantifies this coupling using transfer entropy, which measures information flow between sensory inputs and behavioral outputs. Information flow from sensory inputs to behavior defines a "reactive" component of a navigational strategy, whereas information flow from behavior to sensory inputs defines an "active" component, whereby actions shape subsequent sensory experiences. Analyzing these bidirectional information flows enables us to both predict navigational performance and dissect navigation strategies from trajectories. Using a minimal model that captures the active and reactive components, we connect macroscopic performance to microscopic information flows. We then apply the framework to experimentally measured trajectories of bacteria, worms, and flies, as well as to machine learning agents navigating sensory landscapes. Across systems, bidirectional information flow reliably predicts navigation efficiency, revealing a common behavioral-environment feedback loop. Decomposing active and reactive information flows further exposes distinct strategies underlying bacterial chemotaxis, the spatial dependency of the navigation strategy in fly olfactory navigation, and the learned policies of a reinforcement-trained agent. Together, these results establish bidirectional information flow as a unifying principle for understanding navigation in biological and artificial systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an information-theoretic framework using transfer entropy to quantify bidirectional information flow (reactive and active components) between sensory inputs and behavioral outputs during navigation. The framework predicts navigation efficiency and dissects strategies across bacteria, worms, flies, and AI agents, revealing a universal behavioral-environment feedback loop.
AI.motivation: To understand how organisms tightly couple sensory inputs with behavioral actions during navigation, and to develop a quantitative framework that can predict navigational performance and reveal underlying strategies across diverse biological and artificial systems.
AI.method: The authors use transfer entropy to measure bidirectional information flow: reactive (sensory→behavior) and active (behavior→sensory) components. They develop a minimal model and apply the framework to experimental trajectories of bacteria, worms, flies, and reinforcement learning agents navigating sensory landscapes.
AI.result: Bidirectional information flow reliably predicts navigation efficiency across all systems. Different navigation strategies (bacterial chemotaxis, fly olfactory navigation, RL agent policies) are exposed by decomposing active and reactive information flows. A common behavioral-environment feedback loop is identified.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional information flow serves as a unifying principle for understanding navigation in both biological and artificial systems, establishing a common framework to analyze and compare diverse navigational strategies.

title: Pragmatic Reasoning in Design
comment: Accepted with oral presentation at CogSci 2026
summary: People can often understand and use novel artifacts after only a few interactions, suggesting that design choices communicate underlying affordances and causal structure. We propose a formal account of this process by framing cooperative, user-centered design as a cooperative game in which the user is the principal and the designer is an assistant. Inspired by prior work on pragmatic communication (e.g. RSA), our model treats a designer's design decisions as communicative signals and predicts user judgments via recursive mentalizing: designers make design decisions to trade off informativeness about the artifact with efficiency, and users infer the true model of the artifact by inverting this cooperative designer model. We evaluate the model in a design game where designers place visually identical keys on trays to help a user infer which keys unlock which doors in grid-world layouts. We find that pragmatic designer and user models better match human judgments than non-mentalizing literal baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a formal model of user-centered design as a cooperative game where designers' design choices communicate underlying affordances. Using recursive mentalizing (inspired by RSA), the model treats designers as balancing informativeness with efficiency, while users infer artifact models by inverting this reasoning. Evaluated in a key-door placement game, the pragmatic model outperforms non-mentalizing baselines in matching human judgments.
AI.motivation: To provide a formal account of how people can understand novel artifacts after minimal interactions, by framing user-centered design as cooperative communication where design choices reveal causal structure.
AI.method: A computational model based on recursive mentalizing (RSA framework) where designers optimize trade-offs between informativeness and efficiency, and users infer artifact functionality by inverting the designer's decision process. Tested via a grid-world key-door placement game.
AI.result: The pragmatic (cooperative, mentalizing) designer and user models better match human judgments than non-mentalizing literal baselines.
AI.conclusion: Framing user-centered design as a cooperative game with recursive reasoning between designer and user effectively captures how design choices communicate affordances, and pragmatic models outperform literal baselines.

title: Q-Steer: Action-Value Guidance for Molecular Policy Optimization
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, and 25 tables. Includes supplementary experimental results
summary: Oracle-limited molecular optimization gives reward only after a complete molecule is generated, while each rollout requires many local next-token decisions. This delayed-feedback interface makes molecular policy optimization myopic: an optimizer can learn that a molecule was good without knowing which intermediate actions made it good. We introduce Q-Steer, a rollout-time action-value steering primitive for molecular language models. Q-Steer uses an offline-trained and frozen prefix-action value scorer, PAVS-Q, that estimates the downstream reward of taking a candidate next token under a partial SMILES prefix, then adds a normalized value bonus to sampling logits. The optimizer update rule and online oracle budget are unchanged; the claim is fixed-online-oracle performance, not equal total compute. On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call online budget, complete factorial studies across two molecular language-model backbones and four optimizers show that Q-Steer improves mean valid-unique score in all eight backbone-optimizer cells, with positive macro mean-score gains between +0.033 and +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Mechanism controls show that action identity matters: prefix-broadcast values are nearly neutral, while shuffled action values harm performance. These results support Q-Steer as a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across optimizer families and policy backbones without changing the online oracle budget.

AI.tldr: Q-Steer is a rollout-time action-value steering method that uses an offline-trained prefix-action value scorer (PAVS-Q) to add normalized value bonuses to sampling logits, improving molecular optimization across 8 backbone-optimizer combinations with a fixed 10,000-call online oracle budget.
AI.motivation: Oracle-limited molecular optimization suffers from delayed feedback (reward only after full molecule generation), making policy optimization myopic since the optimizer cannot attribute which intermediate actions led to good outcomes.
AI.method: Q-Steer uses an offline-trained, frozen prefix-action value scorer (PAVS-Q) to estimate downstream rewards of candidate next tokens under partial SMILES prefixes, then adds a normalized value bonus to sampling logits without changing the optimizer or online oracle budget.
AI.result: On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call budget, Q-Steer improves mean valid-unique scores in all 8 backbone-optimizer cells, with positive macro mean-score gains between +0.033 and +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Mechanism controls confirm action identity matters (prefix-broadcast values are neutral, shuffled values harm performance).
AI.conclusion: Q-Steer is a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across optimizer families and policy backbones without increasing the online oracle budget.

title: Knowledge before Reasoning: EC-Reason-Bench, a Training-Free Diagnostic Benchmark for LLM Enzyme Classification
summary: Enzyme function prediction is a hierarchical, knowledge-intensive form of protein function classification. Existing benchmarks expose an anomaly: general LLMs often get the coarse first level right, yet once asked for a complete EC number their accuracy at levels two through four drops to almost zero, while specialized models and tools stay usable. We propose EC-Reason-Bench, a training-free, diagnostic evaluation protocol built to answer two questions: why general LLMs score close to nothing on EC number prediction, and how much of that loss can be recovered without updating a single weight. We break enzyme classification ability into four orthogonal levers that can each be measured on their own: output structure, external knowledge, reasoning structure, and reasoning robustness. We test each lever with an inference-time method against a shared zero-shot baseline reproducing previously reported near-zero performance. Experiments with several strong reasoning LLMs yield four main findings. First, external knowledge is decisive and must precede reasoning: uniformly low closed-book performance rises sharply with open-book access, narrowing model gaps. Second, in closed-book settings, whether cascading and chain-of-thought help or hurt depends on a model's tendency to abstain. Third, once evidence is available the aggregate score of the best LLM setting is indistinguishable from simply voting the EC numbers of the nearest retrieved neighbors; that tie is an artifact of averaging, and it hides a large gain on adversarial evidence set against an equally large loss on multi-functional enzymes. Reasoning over evidence therefore acts as an arbiter of conflicting neighbors rather than as a source of knowledge, and no single-number leaderboard can see it. Fourth, accuracy obeys a law of homology availability.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses why general LLMs fail at enzyme function prediction (EC numbers) and proposes EC-Reason-Bench, a training-free evaluation protocol. Key findings: external knowledge is decisive; open-book access closes the gap with specialized models; reasoning acts as an arbiter of conflicting neighbors rather than a knowledge source; and accuracy follows a law of homology availability.
AI.motivation: General LLMs perform near zero on complete EC number prediction (levels 2-4) despite getting coarse level-1 right, while specialized models remain usable. The paper aims to explain this anomaly and quantify how much can be recovered without weight updates.
AI.method: EC-Reason-Bench breaks enzyme classification into four orthogonal levers: output structure, external knowledge, reasoning structure, and reasoning robustness. Each lever is tested with inference-time methods against a zero-shot baseline, using strong reasoning LLMs.
AI.result: (1) External knowledge is decisive and must precede reasoning; open-book access sharply improves performance. (2) Cascade/COT effects depend on model abstention. (3) Best LLM aggregate matches nearest-neighbor voting, but this masks gains on adversarial evidence vs. losses on multi-functional enzymes. (4) Accuracy obeys a law of homology availability.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning over evidence acts as an arbiter of conflicting neighbors, not a knowledge source. No single-number leaderboard captures this nuance. The findings suggest that for EC prediction, retrieval augmentation is more impactful than reasoning improvements.

title: Navigation driven by bidirectional information transmission between sensing and actuation
summary: A wide variety of biological functions are driven by feedback between sensing and actuation. A paradigmatic example is cellular navigation. During navigation, the sensory system maps the environmental input signal onto a sensory output, which then drives an actuation response, changing the future sensory input. How the accuracy of this bidirectional information transmission controls navigation is not currently understood. Here, we study how information controls navigation by analytically solving two generic models that describe two major classes of biological navigators: spatial- and temporal-sensing cells. We find that, in the linear-response regime of shallow gradients, navigation performance is fully determined by the strengths and timescales of bidirectional information transmission, without any explicit dependence on the elementary parameters of the navigator. We call these relations Behavioral Equations of State (BESTs): equalities that map information to function in a system-independent way. BESTs predict an experimentally testable data collapse for the performance of navigators with different sensing and actuation parameters. We test the validity of our theory by performing stochastic simulations of chemotaxis of the bacterium Escherichia coli, computing transfer entropies exactly with the TE-PWS algorithm. The observed performance obeys the BEST without fitting or scaling parameters. Thus, our theory identifies bidirectional information transmission between sensing and actuation as an organizing principle for navigation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how bidirectional information transmission between sensing and actuation controls biological navigation, deriving Behavioral Equations of State (BESTs) that map information to navigation performance independently of system parameters, validated with E. coli chemotaxis simulations.
AI.motivation: The accuracy of bidirectional information transmission between sensing and actuation in biological navigation is not well understood. The authors aim to find an organizing principle that links information flow to navigation function across different biological systems.
AI.method: Analytically solving two generic models for spatial-sensing and temporal-sensing cells in the linear-response regime (shallow gradients), deriving BESTs. Validated using stochastic simulations of E. coli chemotaxis with the TE-PWS algorithm for computing transfer entropies.
AI.result: Navigation performance is fully determined by strengths and timescales of bidirectional information transmission, independent of elementary parameters. BESTs predict a data collapse for navigators with different parameters, confirmed by E. coli simulations without fitting.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional information transmission between sensing and actuation serves as an organizing principle for navigation, captured by system-independent BESTs.

title: TREA-Net: A Transferable Residual Epidemiological Adaptation Network for Dengue Incidence Forecasting
summary: Accurate multi-week dengue forecasting supports timely vector-control interventions, outbreak preparedness, and healthcare resource allocation. However, newly established surveillance systems often lack the historical data needed to train reliable neural forecasting models. Although pretrained time-series models offer promising zero-shot forecasts, their cross-domain training may not capture local epidemiological dynamics. We propose TREA-Net, a Transferable Residual Epidemiological Adaptation Network for dengue forecasting under limited data. TREA-Net augments neural forecasting backbones with projections from an Environmental Time-Series Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model and learns a lightweight gated residual correction transferable from data-rich to data-scarce regions. Its node-invariant design accommodates surveillance systems with different numbers of locations, while target adaptation requires learning only two global parameters. We transfer knowledge from long-running dengue surveillance in Colombia and Nicaragua to 8-week-ahead forecasting in Mexico and Malaysia using only 78 or 104 weeks of target data. Across five neural backbones and ten transfer settings, TREA-Net improves the corresponding backbone in 9 out of 10 settings, with statistically significant gains. When integrated with TiRex, a foundation model for forecasting, it achieves the lowest mean absolute error across all target datasets. Conformal prediction further maintains empirical coverage while reducing 8-week prediction-interval width by 29.6% in Mexico. These results demonstrate TREA-Net's potential as a lightweight and portable early-warning framework for health agencies with limited surveillance data.

AI.tldr: TREA-Net is a transferable framework that augments neural forecasting backbones with epidemiological model projections and lightweight gated residual correction, enabling accurate multi-week dengue forecasting in data-scarce regions by transferring knowledge from data-rich regions.
AI.motivation: Newly established dengue surveillance systems lack sufficient historical data to train reliable neural forecasting models, while pretrained time-series models trained on cross-domain data fail to capture local epidemiological dynamics.
AI.method: TREA-Net augments neural forecasting backbones with ETS-SIR model projections and learns a lightweight gated residual correction transferable from data-rich to data-scarce regions. It uses node-invariant design to handle different numbers of surveillance locations and requires only two global parameters for target adaptation.
AI.result: Across 5 neural backbones and 10 transfer settings, TREA-Net improves the backbone in 9/10 settings with statistical significance. Integrated with TiRex, it achieves the lowest MAE across all target datasets. Conformal prediction reduces 8-week prediction-interval width by 29.6% in Mexico while maintaining coverage.
AI.conclusion: TREA-Net demonstrates potential as a lightweight and portable early-warning framework for health agencies with limited surveillance data.
